cards.title: Weak automatability of Resolution
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, running in time polynomial in \(|F|+s\), that on input a CNF formula \(F\) and a unary proof budget \(1^{s}\) distinguishes the following two promised cases: \(F\) is satisfiable, or \(F\) has a Resolution refutation with at most \(s\) clauses?

cards.why: Asks whether the existence of a short familiar refutation can make unsatisfiability efficiently recognizable even when finding a refutation in that same calculus is hard. This isolates an unresolved limitation of proof search and the theoretical analysis of SAT solvers.
cards.status_note: Read the complete original abstract, the full regular-Resolution definitions and weak-automatability corollary, the Atserias–Müller author-version main theorems, and the May 2026 full-paper weak-automatability discussion and definitions. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution. The unary-budget promise formulation makes the original distinction precise; no strong-automatability hardness claim has been transferred to it.

progress.text: The author version proves NP-hardness of strong Resolution automatability and of distinguishing short from sufficiently long refutations.
The STACS invited talk explicitly leaves SAT-versus-short-Resolution-refutation separation open.
The revised full Proof Analysis Problem paper continues to discuss weak automatability as an open question.

sentences: The input is a CNF formula and a proof-length budget written in unary.
The algorithm must distinguish satisfiable formulas from those having a short general Resolution refutation.
The proof is not supplied, and the algorithm need not produce a Resolution proof.
Unsatisfiable formulas whose shortest refutations exceed the budget can receive either answer.
Known hardness for finding Resolution proofs does not settle this weaker recognition problem.

cards.definitions:
A CNF formula is an explicit conjunction of clauses over finitely many Boolean variables. Each clause is a disjunction of literals, where a literal is a variable or its negation. Let \(|F|\) be its ordinary binary encoding length, including literal indices and clause boundaries. Variables may be renamed consecutively in polynomial time.

A Resolution derivation is a finite sequence of clauses. Each line is an input clause of \(F\), or follows from two earlier lines by
\[\frac{A\lor x\qquad B\lor\neg x}{A\lor B},\]
where neither \(A\) nor \(B\) contains the pivot variable \(x\). Repeated literals are identified. A refutation ends in the empty clause, which is false under every assignment. Its length is the number of clauses in the sequence. Earlier lines may be reused: this is general directed-acyclic-graph Resolution, with no tree-like or regularity restriction.

The integer \(s\geq1\) is encoded in unary, so the input length is proportional to \(|F|+s\). The short refutation is promised to exist but is not given to the algorithm. Counting total proof symbols instead of clauses changes this polynomial-time question only by polynomial factors, since every clause uses variables of \(F\).

One fixed uniform deterministic algorithm must halt within a fixed polynomial bound on every input. It must output SAT whenever \(F\) is satisfiable, and UNSAT whenever \(F\) has a refutation of length at most \(s\). These cases are disjoint by soundness of Resolution. If \(F\) is unsatisfiable but all its Resolution refutations have length greater than \(s\), either output is allowed. Malformed encodings can be rejected immediately.

No satisfying assignment or refutation has to be output. In particular, the task does not ask whether a refutation of length at most \(s\) exists on every input: an UNSAT output is allowed even when all Resolution refutations are longer. This promise distinction is the decision formulation of weak automatability, corresponding to allowing efficiently checkable proofs in another fixed proof system instead of insisting on Resolution output.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct the stated deterministic polynomial-time separator, or prove that no such separator exists. A conditional obstruction must state its hypothesis explicitly. Hardness of finding a Resolution refutation, estimating its minimum length, or solving unrestricted SAT does not establish hardness of this particular promise separator without a reduction that respects its two promised cases.

context_blocks.title: Strong automatability has a known obstruction
context_blocks.text: Atserias and Müller show that finding a Resolution refutation in time polynomial in the formula size and the shortest available refutation length would imply \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). Their proof-length gap distinguishes short refutations from very long or nonexistent ones. The latter side may include unsatisfiable formulas, so it does not give the SAT-versus-short-refutation promise required here.

context_blocks.title: The distinction survives restrictions on proof shape
context_blocks.text: Buss and Yolcu show that weak automatability of regular Resolution would imply weak automatability of general Resolution. Their definition allows the output proof to use another system. This relation between systems is not an algorithm or a hardness result for the full promise problem.

context_blocks.title: Recent work retains the weak question
context_blocks.text: The May 2026 full version of The Proof Analysis Problem develops algorithms that analyze supplied proofs of Resolution lower bounds. Section 1.4 still treats weak automatability of Resolution as open. Having such an additional proof as input is a different task from receiving only a formula and a unary budget.

cards.context:
Atserias and Müller show that finding a Resolution refutation in time polynomial in the formula size and the shortest available refutation length would imply \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). Their proof-length gap distinguishes short refutations from very long or nonexistent ones. The latter side may include unsatisfiable formulas, so it does not give the SAT-versus-short-refutation promise required here.

Buss and Yolcu show that weak automatability of regular Resolution would imply weak automatability of general Resolution. Their definition allows the output proof to use another system. This relation between systems is not an algorithm or a hardness result for the full promise problem.

The May 2026 full version of The Proof Analysis Problem develops algorithms that analyze supplied proofs of Resolution lower bounds. Section 1.4 still treats weak automatability of Resolution as open. Having such an additional proof as input is a different task from receiving only a formula and a unary budget.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
